question: We have recently been witnessing a series of fervent street protests organised by farmers across Europe. Their main demand is for a change in current EU policy and support for European agriculture. They are protesting against the punishing environmental regulations and burdensome bureaucracy of EU policies and the new CAP.

In addition, high prices and inflation have caused the cost of fertilisers, fuel and electricity to sky-rocket, making the average cost of farming in the EU unsustainable. Farmers are also protesting against unfair competition from products that are imported from non-EU countries.

The deferral of customs duties on imports from Ukraine has already caused imports to double and countries such as Morocco as well as states in North America are not subject to the EU’s strict rules, making their producers far more competitive compared to EU farmers. In view of this: 1.
In light of the Commission's concession involving the temporary suspension of the set-aside scheme, does it intend to take further steps to alleviate the cost of farming in the EU?
How will it address unfair competition from non-EU countries and support European farmers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.4.2024) 1. The Commission launched a thorough analysis of the administrative burden weighting on farmers’ shoulders to identify areas for improvement. The first set of actions1 includes e.g.

, simplifying some of the conditionality requirements with which EU farmers need to comply2, reviewing the monitoring and control arrangements and clarifying the use of the concept of force majeure and exceptional circumstances. The Commission also launched a study on simplification, including a survey3 addressed to farmers. 2.
Food and feed imported into the EU must comply with all EU sanitary requirements, with checks carried out at EU border control posts.

Moreover, the EU has adopted or proposed to adopt several autonomous measures – in compliance with our international obligations imposing on all products placed on the EU market, including imports, additional EU standards related to process and production methods to address global environmental or ethical concerns4.
Besides, all recent EU trade agreements include commitments to implement ratified international labour conventions and multilateral environmental agreements.

The study on the cumulative economic impact of future trade agreements on EU agriculture5 predicts an overall increase in the EU’s agricultural trade balance through implementation of ten upcoming agreements, whilst suggesting adaptation of market access concessions to the sensitivity of EU sectors.

Where applicable, safeguard clauses may remedy serious injury or disturbances to the domestic industry caused by imports. Any EU industry harmed by unfairly dumped or subsidized imports may seek advice from the DirectorateGeneral for Trade of the Commission regarding the EU trade defence instruments.

Maximum Residues Level on two neonicotinoids contributing to the decline of pollinator; the Regulation on veterinary medicinal products, which prohibits the use of antibiotic as growth promoter for imported products; the new directive on corporate sustainability due diligence. 5 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC135540, February 2024.
